blocks.text: Before making Search smarter, we needed to make it work.
blocks.note: Search is a key route to discovering and launching games across Paddy Power, Betfair and Sky Vegas, but the existing experience wasn’t consistently helping players find the right game quickly. The opportunity wasn’t simply to redesign the interface. It was to establish reliable foundations while exploring how Search could support different player needs and brand identities.

blocks.heading: Auditing the current experience
blocks.text: An audit of the live experience captured specific pain points: search wasn’t instant, results only appeared after three letters, and a relevant game, Big Bass 2, didn’t appear in the list.

blocks.heading: Two different needs. One Search experience.
paragraphs: Research and analytics suggested two broad ways players use Search. The design needed to serve both.

blocks.heading: March 2026 — Informal cross-functional conversations
paragraphs: I initiated conversations across Product, Development, Data, Content, Design and Commercial to understand how colleagues use Search in everyday life and what they expect from a good search experience.
These weren’t formal user interviews. They were a way to surface assumptions, challenge internal thinking and bring different perspectives into the discussion.

blocks.heading: March 2026 — User Needs & Wants
paragraphs: Dedicated UX Research then strengthened our understanding of player expectations and informed further design exploration.

blocks.heading: Thinking beyond the search bar.
paragraphs: A Product-led ideation workshop in March 2026 explored what a more ambitious discovery experience might look like. It brought together behavioural signals, player needs, technical opportunities and ideas from other digital products.

blocks.heading: Themes that emerged
items: Understanding intent, not only matching keywords
Exploratory concepts such as mood-based search

paragraphs: These were opportunities for exploration, not confirmed or delivered functionality. The workshop gave us a broader opportunity space and candidate ideas for further design, prototyping and validation.

blocks.heading: Fix what matters before changing how it looks.
paragraphs: The initial design direction concentrated on search fundamentals rather than introducing every exploratory feature. A more polished interface wouldn’t fix slow or inaccurate results.
A phased approach let us introduce improvements progressively and learn before deciding what came next.

blocks.heading: Design direction: evolution, not reinvention
paragraphs: From the outset, I didn’t believe Search needed a complete visual overhaul. The biggest problems weren’t how it looked, but how it worked.
My approach was to keep things simple: build on existing components and patterns, improve the core experience and avoid introducing complexity where it wasn’t needed.
We started with a two-tile results layout because it allowed us to use existing game-tile components and move forward without waiting for a completely new system.

The longer-term direction is a three-tile layout, but rather than jumping straight to the intended end state, we wanted to learn from the initial approach and use that evidence to inform the next iteration.

blocks.heading: A shared experience, without losing brand identity.
paragraphs: Working across Paddy Power, Betfair and Sky Vegas meant balancing consistency with individuality.
The search functionality and core interaction patterns could be shared, but each brand needed to retain its own personality.
We worked with Brand and Commercial stakeholders throughout the process to understand what mattered to them and where flexibility was needed.
This included differences in typography, tone of voice, colours and existing game-tile treatments, for example Paddy Power’s distinctive green tile borders.

blocks.heading: Looking beyond visual differences
paragraphs: Working with Data and other teams, we also wanted to understand differences in search behaviour across the brands.

The ambition is for the shared system to support more relevant, context-aware experiences rather than assuming players across every brand are looking for the same games. The foundations can remain consistent while the experience becomes increasingly relevant to each audience.
This is an ongoing direction, not a delivered personalisation capability.

blocks.heading: Turning uncertainty into a shared direction.
paragraphs: A later in-person workshop in August brought Product, Design, the Product Owner and Engineering together to work through refreshed GA4 evidence, existing UXR and technical considerations.

images.alt: Product, Design and Engineering working through search and filtering at the in-person workshop
Whiteboard comparing the current and proposed filtering flows

blocks.caption: Working through search and filtering together at the in-person workshop.

paragraphs: One important shift was reframing the filtering question. Rather than deciding only whether filters should appear before or after searching, the team considered how Search and filtering could operate independently while complementing one another.
The workshop also progressed discovery around promotional eligibility and richer Search capabilities. These remain areas of exploration, not delivered outcomes.

blocks.heading: Reflection
paragraphs: The most useful decisions came from balancing ambition with foundational quality, and from bringing the right disciplines into the same room.
